transcript:
"This is NPR News Now."
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Rylan Barton.
A sell-off swept through Wall Street today, led by stocks tied to A.I., worries rose about
possible moratoriums on data centers following Democratic victories in the midterm elections.
The S&P 500 fell more than 4.25 percent, the worst drop since President Trump's Liberation
Day tariffs.
The Dow dropped more than 1,800 points, nearly 3.5 percent.
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's future may be up in the air.
Outgoing Republican Congressman Thomas Massie says he's drawing up articles of impeachment.
Today, Hegseth released a defiant video.
Their policies don't work, so their obsession with political theater disguised as power
drives them to try to destroy their opponents.
It's all about the politics of personal destruction.
Didn't work against President Trump, and it won't work with me.
Hegseth was a key architect of President Trump's unpopular Iran war.
Trump told reporters yesterday that he's not considering replacing Hegseth.
Hegseth has been mentioned as a potential appointed senator in Tennessee, where Republican
Senator Marshall Blackburn won the governor's race and could pick her interim successor.
The midterms brought record wins for Democratic women, but as NPR's Windsor-Johnson reports,
there will be fewer Republican women in Congress.
At least 108 Democratic women will serve in the next Congress, up from 95 today.
For Republican women, the numbers are moving in the opposite direction.
30 hold seats now, but only 17 have won so far, with some races still undecided.
All told, women will make up 28 percent of the House.
Voters also broke barriers in gubernatorial races.
In Georgia, Keisha Lance Bottoms will become the nation's first black woman governor.
In Texas, Gina Inajosa will be the state's first Latina governor.
And in New Mexico, Deb Haaland's victory marks the first for a Native American female.
They'll join a record group of 17 women from both parties occupying governor's mansions
next year.
Windsor-Johnson, NPR News.
Democratic Socialist Nithya Rahman will be Los Angeles' next mayor, defeating incumbent
Karen Bass, Steve Futterman reports.
The concession by Mayor Bass came after numbers showed Nithya Rahman's lead increasing.
Even though there are still many votes to be counted, Bass concluded there was no realistic
way for her to win.
In a statement, Bass said, while this is not the outcome she hoped for, the people of Los
Angeles have spoken.
She promised a smooth transition.
Soon after, Mayor-elect Rahman made a statement on social media.
Thank you to the thousands of people who knocked on doors, convinced their neighbors to believe
in the promise of this big, beautiful, joyful city that we get to call home.
Rahman will become Los Angeles' first Asian-American mayor.
A key issue in the campaign was Bass's handling of last year's deadly Palisades fire.
For NPR News, I'm Steve Futterman in Los Angeles.
This is NPR News from Washington.
Police say that bomb threats have targeted more than a dozen flights in Europe, leading
to emergency landings and military escorts in some cases.
No hazardous or suspicious materials have been found in what a British official called
"malicious hoaxes."
Several similar threats targeted planes earlier this week, prompting searches and diversions.
A new report finds a record share of first-time homebuyers are paying with all cash, and PRS
Jennifer Ludden explains some are able to do that because they got inheritance.
Ten in ten first-time homebuyers pay all cash, according to the National Association of Realtors,
and more than a quarter of them use inherited money.
NAR Deputy Chief Economist Jessica Lautz says they're also significantly older than traditional
first-time buyers, with a median age of 54.
They waited a significant period of time for that generational transfer of wealth to come
through.
Real estate agents say intense competition and sky-high interest rates are driving all
cash offers, and of course some families don't wait until death to pass on money.
The report notes it's all widening the divide between homebuyers and those priced out.
Jennifer Ludden, NPR News, Washington.
Chihuahuas carry about 4 percent wild coyote ancestry in their genome, according to a Stanford
study published in Nature Communications.
Unlike most dog breeds that trace their lineage back to old-world wolves, Chihuahuas retain
genetic fragments from pre-contact American canines.
The genetic heritage is believed to pass down through the tachichi, an extinct, small, barkless
companion dog domesticated by ancient civilizations in Mexico.
I'm Rylan Barton, this is NPR News.

topics.text: Wall Street sell-off led by A.I. stocks amid worries over data center moratoriums; S&P 500 falls over 4%
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's job in doubt as Congressman Thomas Massie drafts impeachment articles
Hegseth releases defiant video; Trump says he is not considering replacing him
Hegseth mentioned as possible appointed senator in Tennessee after Marshall Blackburn wins governor's race
Record number of Democratic women to serve in next Congress while Republican women's numbers fall
Keisha Lance Bottoms, Gina Inajosa, and Deb Haaland win governor races in Georgia, Texas, and New Mexico
Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass concedes to Democratic Socialist Nithya Rahman, who becomes first Asian-American mayor
Bomb threats target more than a dozen flights in Europe, causing emergency landings; no hazardous materials found
Record share of first-time homebuyers paying all cash, many using inherited money, NAR report finds
Stanford study finds Chihuahuas carry about 4 percent wild coyote ancestry in their genome
